blocks.content: While ENV in a Dockerfile bakes a default into the image, most real environment configuration actually happens at runtime, injected into a container the moment it starts, without ever touching the image itself.

docker run -e KEY=value sets an environment variable for that specific container, visible to its process from the moment it starts, entirely independent of whatever the image's Dockerfile did or did not declare with ENV.

blocks.alt: A variable injected fresh, at container start

blocks.content: Nothing limits you to one -e flag, a real production docker run command commonly carries several, one per variable the application needs configured for that specific environment.

blocks.alt: As many -e flags as the application needs

blocks.content: 3. Overriding What the Image Already Baked In
blocks.text: 3. Overriding What the Image Already Baked In

blocks.content: As covered in the Dockerfile module's ENV topic, a runtime -e value takes priority over whatever default the image's ENV instruction set, this is exactly how the same image runs correctly configured for dev, staging, and production without ever needing to be rebuilt.

blocks.alt: A runtime override, no rebuild required

blocks.content: 4. Loading Many Variables from a File
blocks.text: 4. Loading Many Variables from a File

blocks.content: Typing a dozen -e flags by hand gets unwieldy fast, --env-file loads an entire file of KEY=VALUE lines in one shot, covered in full in the next topic.

blocks.alt: One flag, an entire file of variables loaded at once

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: -e injects an environment variable at container start, overriding whatever default an image's ENV instruction baked in.
This is the standard way the same image is configured differently across dev, staging, and production, no rebuild required.
